mn146:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
mn146:2.1: Then Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, together with about five hundred bhikkhunīs, went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, she stood at one side. Standing at one side, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī said to the Blessed One:
mn146:2.2: ‘Venerable sir, let the Blessed One advise the bhikkhunīs;
mn146:2.3: let the Blessed One instruct the bhikkhunīs;
mn146:2.4: let the Blessed One give the bhikkhunīs a talk on the Dhamma.’
mn146:3.1: Now on that occasion the elder bhikkhus were advising the bhikkhunīs in turn.
mn146:3.2: The venerable Nandaka did not want to advise the bhikkhunīs in his turn.
mn146:3.3: Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda thus:
mn146:3.4: ‘Ānanda, whose turn is it today to advise the bhikkhunīs?’
mn146:3.5: ‘Venerable sir, it is everyone’s turn to advise the bhikkhunīs.
mn146:3.6: It is the venerable Nandaka’s turn, venerable sir, but he does not want to advise the bhikkhunīs.’
mn146:4.1: Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Nandaka thus:
mn146:4.4: give the bhikkhunīs a talk on the Dhamma, brahmin.’
mn146:4.5: ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ the venerable Nandaka replied to the Blessed One. Then, when it was morning, he dressed, and taking his bowl and outer robe, went into Sāvatthī for alms.
mn146:4.6: When he had wandered for alms in Sāvatthī and had returned from his alms round, after the meal he went with a companion to the Rājaka Park.
mn146:4.7: The bhikkhunīs saw the venerable Nandaka coming from a distance.
mn146:4.8: Seeing him, they prepared a seat and set out water for the feet.
mn146:4.9: The venerable Nandaka sat down on the seat made ready.
mn146:4.10: Having sat down, he washed his feet.
mn146:4.11: Those bhikkhunīs paid homage to the venerable Nandaka and sat down at one side.
mn146:4.12: The venerable Nandaka said this to those bhikkhunīs sitting at one side:
mn146:5.1: ‘This talk will be in the form of questions, sisters.
mn146:5.2: When you know, you should say: “We know”; when you do not know, you should say: “We do not know”.
mn146:5.3: Or if any of you has doubt or uncertainty, I too should be questioned thus:
mn146:5.4: “Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this?”’
mn146:5.5: ‘Venerable sir, we are satisfied and pleased that the venerable Nandaka invites us in this way.’

mn146:9.1: Sisters, suppose there were an oil lamp burning: its oil would be impermanent and subject to change, its wick would be impermanent and subject to change, its flame would be impermanent and subject to change, and its radiance would be impermanent and subject to change.
mn146:9.2: If anyone were to say, sisters:
mn146:9.3: “While that oil lamp is burning, its oil is impermanent and subject to change, its wick is impermanent and subject to change, its flame is impermanent and subject to change,
mn146:9.4: but its radiance is permanent, everlasting, eternal, and not subject to change”—
mn146:9.5: would he be speaking rightly, sisters?’
mn146:9.8: ‘Because, venerable sir, while that oil lamp is burning, its oil is impermanent and subject to change, its wick is impermanent and subject to change, its flame is impermanent and subject to change,
mn146:9.9: so how much more its radiance, which is impermanent and subject to change.’
mn146:9.10: ‘So too, sisters, if anyone were to say:
mn146:9.11: “These six bases in oneself are impermanent,
mn146:9.12: but that pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling which one experiences dependent on the six bases in oneself is permanent, everlasting, eternal, and not subject to change”—
mn146:9.13: would he be speaking rightly, sisters?’
mn146:9.16: ‘Because, venerable sir, each appropriate feeling arises dependent on its appropriate condition,
mn146:9.17: and with the cessation of its appropriate condition, that appropriate feeling ceases.’
mn146:9.19: So it is, sisters, for a noble disciple who sees this as it actually is with right understanding.

mn146:11.1: Sisters, suppose a clever butcher or his apprentice, having killed a cow, were to carve it up with a sharp carving knife, without damaging the inner mass of flesh and without damaging the outer hide,
mn146:11.2: and whatever inner tissue, sinews, and ligaments there were, he would cut, sever, and carve them all away with the sharp carving knife;
mn146:11.3: and having cut, severed, and carved them all away, having removed the outer hide, he were to cover that cow again with that same hide and say:
mn146:11.4: “This cow is joined to this hide just as before”—
mn146:11.5: would he be speaking rightly, sisters?’
mn146:11.8: ‘Because, venerable sir, however much that clever butcher or his apprentice, having killed that cow, were to carve it up with a sharp carving knife, without damaging the inner mass of flesh and without damaging the outer hide,
mn146:11.9: and whatever inner tissue, sinews, and ligaments there were, he were to cut, sever, and carve them all away with the sharp carving knife;
mn146:11.10: and having cut, severed, and carved them all away, having removed the outer hide, were to cover that cow again with that same hide and say:

mn146:12.1: ‘This simile, sisters, has been made by me to convey a meaning.
mn146:12.2: And this is the meaning here:
mn146:12.3: “the inner mass of flesh,” sisters, is a term for the six bases in oneself;
mn146:12.4: “the outer hide,” sisters, is a term for the six external bases;
mn146:12.5: “the inner tissue, sinews, and ligaments,” sisters, is a term for relishing and lust;
mn146:12.6: “the sharp carving knife,” sisters, is a term for noble understanding—
mn146:12.7: the noble understanding that cuts, severs, and carves away the inner defilements, fetters, and bonds.
mn146:13.1: ‘There are, sisters, these seven enlightenment factors, developing and cultivating which a bhikkhu, by realizing for himself with direct knowledge, here and now enters upon and abides in the taintless deliverance of mind and deliverance by understanding, with the exhaustion of the taints.
mn146:13.3: Here, sisters, a bhikkhu develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor, which is supported by seclusion, by dispassion, by cessation, and ripens in relinquishment.
mn146:13.4: He develops the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor …
mn146:13.5: he develops the energy enlightenment factor …
mn146:13.6: he develops the joy enlightenment factor …
mn146:13.7: he develops the tranquillity enlightenment factor …
mn146:13.8: he develops the concentration enlightenment factor …
mn146:13.9: he develops the equanimity enlightenment factor, which is supported by seclusion, by dispassion, by cessation, and ripens in relinquishment.
mn146:13.10: These, sisters, are the seven enlightenment factors, developing and cultivating which a bhikkhu, by realizing for himself with direct knowledge, here and now enters upon and abides in the taintless deliverance of mind and deliverance by understanding, with the exhaustion of the taints.’

mn146:15.1: Then, not long after those bhikkhunīs had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus thus:
mn146:15.2: ‘Bhikkhus, just as on the fourteenth day of the fortnight, on the observance day, most people have no doubt or uncertainty whether the moon is deficient or full,

mn146:27.1: Then, not long after those bhikkhunīs had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus thus:
mn146:27.2: ‘Bhikkhus, just as on the fifteenth day of the fortnight, on the observance day, most people have no doubt or uncertainty whether the moon is deficient or full,
